idiom_name: protocol with no requirements, conformance declared at the type
implementation_notes: Swift protocols may declare no requirements: conformance is nominal, declared in the type's own file, recorded by the compiler, and ordinary is/as? casts work because the protocol exists at run time as an existential. Declare an empty protocol, add conformance at the type declaration, and constrain generics with it - the classic marker interface with Swift spelling. Retroactive conformance was removed, so types you do not own cannot be marked after the fact.
pitfalls: Conformance can only be declared in the same file as the type, so external types cannot be marked retroactively.
An empty protocol matches by declaration only; there is no structural check, and a typo in the conformance list fails compilation rather than degrading.
Boxing into any Deletable can allocate; prefer generics in hot paths.

variants.name: Compile-time marker protocol (Sendable pattern)
variants.idiom_name: Sendable / @unchecked Sendable from the standard library
variants.implementation_notes: Swift's standard library introduces true marker protocols: Sendable declares no requirements yet is enforced at compile time (stored properties must be Sendable; classes must be final with immutable state), with @unchecked Sendable as the documented escape hatch, and marker protocols have no runtime presence - they cannot even appear in is/as? casts. User-defined marker protocols remain compiler-internal per SE-0302, so application markers use ordinary empty protocols while the stdlib ships true marker protocols. Use Sendable to mark types that may cross concurrency domains.
pitfalls: @unchecked Sendable disables the compiler's checks and transfers the proof obligation to you; a wrong promise causes data races.
Sendable conformance must be in the same file as the type definition, and actor/MainActor types get implicit conformance.
Marker protocols have no runtime presence, so value is Sendable cannot be tested.
